Q: How to get Tkinter and Pygame windows to run at the same time? A:

In tkinter you can try to use window.after(millisecond, function) to process Pygame's event (and redraw window) without while True (which is blocking window.mainloop())

OR

In pygame you can try to use window.update() to force tkinter to process events and redraw widgets in windows without window.mainloop() (which is blocing pygame)

This way you will have only one loop and it doesn't need multiprocessing.

But I don't know if problem is also that you destroy and recreate again tkinter window.

I made full working code which uses window.after() to still process Pygame events.

It needed to use global variable to control when after() should stop running.

(I used pg.event.clear() instead of for event in pg.event.get(): pass)

I also create window Tk() only once and later I use withdraw() to hide it and deiconify() to show it again. I also keep buttons in Frame to simpler remove them from window and replace with other Frame with new buttons.

(instead of .destroy() you can also use .pack_forget() and later it needs only .pack() again to show it)

import tkinter as tk
import pygame as pg


def main():
    global window
    global frame

    frame = None

    # create window only once and run mainloop
    window = tk.Tk()
    set_frame_main_menu()  # at start
    window.mainloop()


def set_frame_main_menu():
    global frame

    if frame is not None:
        frame.destroy()

    print("set_frame_main_menu")
    frame = tk.Frame(window)
    frame.pack()

    button1 = tk.Button(frame, text="Start game", command=run_game)
    button1.pack()

    button2 = tk.Button(frame, text="EXIT", command=window.destroy)
    button2.pack(fill="x")


def set_frame_back_button():
    global frame

    if frame is not None:
        frame.destroy()

    print("set_frame_back_button")
    frame = tk.Frame(window)
    frame.pack()

    button = tk.Button(frame, text="Back to menu", command=go_back_to_main_menu)
    button.pack()


def run_game():
    print("hide tkinter window")
    window.withdraw()  # hide window

    print("play game")
    play_game()

    print("show tkinter window")
    window.deiconify()  # show again window

    print("set back button")
    set_frame_back_button()

    print("keep running Pygame loop")
    # use after() to run look with pygame events without blocking mainloop
    global keep_loop

    keep_loop = True
    keep_pygame_event_loop()  # run at once
    # window.after(100, keep_pygame_event_loop)  # OR run after 100ms


def play_game():
    import random

    pg.init()
    screen = pg.display.set_mode((100, 100))
    clock = pg.time.Clock()

    while True:
        color = random.choice(["red", "green", "blue"])

        for event in pg.event.get():
            if event.type == pg.QUIT:
                return

        screen.fill(color)
        pg.display.flip()
        clock.tick(10)


def keep_pygame_event_loop():
    global keep_loop

    if keep_loop:
        pg.event.clear()  # get all events and do nothing
        window.after(100, keep_pygame_event_loop)  # run again after 100ms
    else:
        pg.quit()


def go_back_to_main_menu():
    global keep_loop

    # stop loop
    keep_loop = False

    set_frame_main_menu()


main()

Q: Update query used the wrong table in the from statement A:

(This was migrated from my earlier comments, after which I noticed that this is amazingly similar to Charlieface's answer.)

To better explain what happened, your update statement had two independent references to the [Pallet Contents] table. The reference inside the CTE was used to retrieve a set of rows and columns that was then given the name productPickLocation. Outside the CTE, the original Pallet Contents table reference is not visible, so when the table name was again referenced in UPDATE [Pallet Contents] ..., a second independent copy was accessed. You effectively had a CROSS JOIN between two copies of the [Pallet Contents] table, updating each row based on data from all other rows.

If you had instead written UPDATE productPickLocation SET productPickLocation.Qty = ..., the update statement would have been applied to the visible productPickLocation referenced in the FROM clause. SQL Server would have then seen through the CTE wrapper and updated the Qty column in the original [Pallet Contents] table reference.

I think what you intended was something like the following (adapted from your earlier posted fiddle):

WITH productPickLocation AS (
    SELECT tpc.*
    FROM PalletContents tpc
    LEFT JOIN Pallet tp ON tpc.PalletID = tp.PalletID
    WHERE tpc.P2CPullLocation = 1 AND tp.WarehouseID = 1
)
UPDATE ppl
SET Qty = ppl.Qty - td.Diff
FROM #TempDiff td
INNER JOIN Products pr ON td.SKU = pr.ItemNumber
LEFT JOIN productPickLocation ppl ON pr.ProductKey = ppl.ProductKey;

Notes:

  • If the CTE reference is given an alias, the UPDATE needs to refer to that alias, not the CTE name. I also added extra test data to demo multiple products and duplicates.
  • The LEFT JOINs above are effectively INNER JOINs. One due to the pallets.WarehouseID = 3 condition that is applied in the CTE and one due to the fact that you can't UPDATE a missing row.

This can also be rewritten without the CTE:

UPDATE pc
SET Qty = pc.Qty - td.Diff
FROM #TempDiff td
INNER JOIN Products pr ON td.SKU = pr.ItemNumber
INNER JOIN PalletContents pc ON pr.ProductKey = pc.ProductKey
INNER JOIN Pallet tp ON pc.PalletID = tp.PalletID
WHERE pc.P2CPullLocation = 1 AND tp.WarehouseID = 1;

I also see a potential problem with the apparent intended logic. Given a SKU and Diff Quantity, you: (1) look up the PRODUCTKEY in the products table, (2) use that to find matching [Pallet Contents] rows, (3) use the PalletID to lookup the matching row in the Pallet table, (4) filter on P2CPullLocation and WarehouseID, and finally, (5) adjust the Qty in the remaining PalletContents rows. The potential problem I see is: What if a given product is stored on more than one pallet in the specified warehouse. Multiple [Pallet Contents] rows could be updated by the same SKU and Diff combo.

See this db<>fiddle for a demo, where I've edited your earlier posted fiddle. I changed the table and column names back to match your original post for consistency (but dropped the spaces from the names for improved readability). I also added extra test data to demo multiple products and duplicates. I'm not posting this as an answer because I think it still needs work.

This may be closer to what you intended, but I cannot guarantee this because my analysis is incomplete. You should revisit your requirements and make sure you have taken into account all of the possible scenarios, such as multiple pallets having the same products.

Q: Why is the compiler ignoring my int assignment operator when I use an integer literal as input? A:

The problem is that the assignment operator you've provided for derived has a non-const lvalue reference parameter of type int& which can't bind to rvalues like 5.

But since you've also provided a converting ctor derived::derived(int), the argument 5 can be implicitly converted to an object of type derived using this converting ctor(hence the name). To avoid this, you can make this converting ctor explicit which will disable the implict conversion of 5 to a temporary derived object. When to make constructor explicit in C++ lists some scenarios like yours, where explicit can/should be used.

How can I fix this

Change the parameter of the assignment operator such that it can bind to rvalues. So, you can either change it to take const int& or int. Both const int& and int will accept rvalues as well as lvalues as argument. Note that there is yet another way of accepting rvalues which is by making the parameter to be of type int&&. This int&& will accept only rvalues i.e this third way won't work if you pass an lvalue as argument(for you particular case, all three ways will work).

Also see When to make assignment operator virtual.
